title: Evolution of Psychological Testing: Pseudoscience, Anthropometrics, Chronometry, Psychometrics
summary: Phrenology (Franz Gall), Anthropometrics (Francis Galton, 1885), Chronometry (Gustav Fechner), Psychometrics (Alfred Binet, 1905); key researchers and contributions.
objectives: Trace the historical evolution of psychological testing.
Identify key researchers and their contributions.
traps: Binet-Simon scale (1905) = first modern intelligence test.
confusions: Mixing up researchers and their contributions.

notes.c: Milestones in the evolution of psychological testing
r: Skull shape as indicator of mental faculties (pseudoscience).
Measurement of physical and sensory characteristics.
Measurement of reaction time and mental chronometry.

notes.t: Phrenology was an early pseudoscientific approach that claimed mental faculties could be determined by the shape and bumps of the skull. Although discredited, it marked the first attempt to localise mental functions.
Francis Galton pioneered the measurement of individual differences through anthropometrics — measuring physical and sensory characteristics such as height, weight, grip strength and reaction time.
Gustav Fechner developed chronometry — the measurement of reaction time as an index of mental processes, founding the experimental study of mental chronometry.

Alfred Binet developed the first modern intelligence test (Binet-Simon scale, 1905) to identify children who needed special educational assistance. This marked the birth of psychometrics — the science of psychological measurement.
UGC NET frequently asks about key researchers and years: Gall (phrenology), Galton (anthropometrics, 1885), Fechner (chronometry), Binet (psychometrics, 1905).
